newsitem.title: USA: Clinton hails drop in U.S. welfare rolls.
newsitem.headline: Clinton hails drop in U.S. welfare rolls.

text.p: President Clinton Tuesday said a one-year drop of 1.4 million persons from welfare rolls showed welfare reform has worked, even though an aide admitted there was no proof the government overhaul caused the decline.
Clinton also worked for the welfare of the debt-ridden Democratic Party -- and was to raise some $550,000 for party coffers by attending events in St. Louis and Washington before the day was done.

Speaking in the sauna-like heat of an old warehouse on a steamy August day, Clinton said the nation's welfare caseload has fallen by 1.4 million recipients in the year since he signed a Republican-backed welfare law.
The law ended the federal government's guarantee of federal aid and led to dire predictions about the future of the underprivileged.
"I heard all the reasons that people said it wouldn't work. But a year later I think it's fair to say the debate is over. We know now that welfare reform works," Clinton said.

Since he took office in January 1993, the number of people receiving welfare benefits fell by 24 percent, or 3.4 million recipients, which Clinton called the largest U.S. decline ever in the welfare rolls.

However, Clinton chief domestic policy adviser, Bruce Reed, acknowledged there was no statistical proof that the welfare changes had any impact on the sharp decline -- noting it will be five years before the full implication of the law can be measured.

Discussing the people who left the benefit rolls in the past year, Reed said: "Most of these people have probably gone to work or gotten married ... We won't know all the facts on this for some time to come."
In Washington, Brookings Institution analyst Robert Reischauer said the drop had more to do with the robust U.S. economy and the flexibility Clinton has given states to administer their programmes.

"The strength of the economy has obviously been a major factor explaining the drop in the welfare rolls," he said, adding: "It is premature to attribute much of the drop in the rolls to the welfare bill because ... the consequences of those changes in most states probably haven't been implemented yet."

Clinton appeared at the welfare event and at a fund-raising luncheon with House Democratic leader Dick Gephardt of Missouri -- a likely rival to Vice President Al Gore for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2000.

Clinton sought to play down his differences with Gephardt -- who opposed both the welfare bill last year and the balanced budget legislation the president signed last week -- and urged the audience to return Democrats to control of the House in elections next year.
"We are within sight of winning the majority in the House," Clinton proclaimed at the affair that raised $250,000 for the Democratic National Committee.

Clinton was to speak Tuesday night in Washington at Democratic dinner raising another $300,000. Some of the contributions at both events were large, unregulated "soft money" donations that Clinton has said he wants to ban as part of campaign finance reform legislation stalled in Congress.
The new welfare law includes requirements that able-bodied welfare recipents find work within two years and people on welfare have a five-year time limit on receiving benefits.

A state-by-state analysis released by the White House on the decline in welfare rolls since 1993 showed wide differences between states. Eleven states saw rolls go down 40 percent or more, led by Wyoming's drop of 68 percent, while California's dropped 1 percent and New York's went down 12 percent. Hawaii's welfare caseloads increased by 36 percent and Alaska's went up 5 percent.
